fullText:
Summary: Sampath Bank (SAMP.N0000) is a well-run, well-capitalised bank, but at today's price it's a little above fair value. At Rs 152 it trades at 0.91x its group NAV of Rs 166.78, so it still passes your NAV rule, and at 5.1x trailing earnings with a 6.8% dividend yield it looks cheap on simple multiples. But a Sri Lankan bank needs a high return to justify owning it (I use an 18% cost of equity), and on that basis the four methods put fair value at about Rs 141, so the price is about 8% above it. I'd buy at up to about Rs 120 and treat under Rs 106 as a strong buy. Profit is growing (group profit up 14% in the first half of 2026), but loans grew 18% in six months, which is using up capital, and the first half was helped by one-offs.

Price and key figures
Price: Rs 152.00, the CSE close on 6 November 2026. It closed at Rs 143.25 on 30 June 2026, after a Q2 range of Rs 137.75–150.75, and reached Rs 167.00 in Q1 2026.
First half of 2026 (group, unaudited): profit after tax rose 14% to Rs 17.9bn. EPS was Rs 15.23 against Rs 13.33. Second-quarter profit rose 65%.
What drove it: net interest income rose 11% (bank Rs 42.8bn; net interest margin 4.21% against 4.11% for 2025), fees rose 26%, and exchange income rose to Rs 7.2bn as the rupee weakened. Against that, impairment charges rose to Rs 5.0bn from Rs 1.2bn because of 18% loan growth and extra provisions, costs rose 21%, and gains on bond sales fell to Rs 1.0bn from Rs 3.5bn. Tax fell 18% because prior-year assessments were finalised, and the second quarter included over Rs 3bn of impairment reversals from recoveries. Both are one-offs.
Balance sheet: gross loans grew Rs 226bn (18%) to Rs 1,449bn; deposits reached Rs 1.76tn. The gross Stage 3 (impaired) loan ratio fell to 6.54% from 8.37%, with 65.6% covered by provisions, but Stage 2 loans rose Rs 36.8bn as the bank reclassified exposures cautiously.
Capital: CET1 fell to 13.21% from 14.75% and total capital to 15.62% from 17.65%, as loan growth used capital. The bank issued a Rs 10bn Basel III green bond in July 2026.
2025 (group): profit Rs 32.6bn (up 13.5%), EPS Rs 27.77, dividend Rs 10.30 (40% of profit, in cash), NAV Rs 165.23. Bank ROE 17.9%.

Methods
NAV (group Rs 166.78): 0.91x, passes your NAV rule. Book value matters more for a bank than for a telecom company.
Return on equity: 18.9% for the first half of 2026, annualised (bank). 2025: 17.9%, 2024: 17.7%, 2023: 12.7%, 2022: 11.0%.
P/E: 5.1x trailing group EPS of Rs 29.67. Bank year-end P/E: 5.7x (2025), 5.1x (2024), 4.8x (2023), 3.0x (2022).
Dividends: Rs 10.30 for 2025, a 6.8% yield, 40% of profit, paid once a year.
Capital and asset quality: CET1 13.21%, total capital 15.62%; gross Stage 3 6.54%, coverage 65.6%.
Justified price to book: Rs 111.2 / 152.9 / 210.7 across the cases, weighted Rs 151.9.
P/E method: Rs 126.0 / 170.5 / 214.5, weighted Rs 165.9.
Dividend model: Rs 71.3 / 106.4 / 147.6, weighted Rs 104.1.
Residual income: Rs 97.7 / 143.4 / 207.1, weighted Rs 142.4.

A bank's cash flows are mostly lending and deposits, so instead of a cash-flow DCF I used residual income, which values the bank as its book value plus the profit it earns above the 18% return investors require. The dividend model is the strictest because the bank keeps 60% of its profit to fund loan growth. The P/E method is the most generous because the base case assumes the market pays 5.5x earnings, close to its recent range.

Assumptions (bear / base / bull)
Cost of equity: 20% / 18% / 16.5%.
Long-run ROE (price to book): 15% / 17% / 19%.
ROE path (residual income): 16.5% falling to 14% / 18% falling to 16% / 19% falling to 18%.
Long-term growth: 5% / 6% / 7%.
2026 EPS × P/E: 28 × 4.5 / 31 × 5.5 / 33 × 6.5.
Dividend per share 2026, then growth for five years: Rs 11.00, 4% / Rs 12.40, 7% / Rs 13.20, 9%.
Average of the four methods: Rs 101.5 / Rs 143.3 / Rs 195.0.
Common: Sri Lankan 7–10-year government bonds yield about 12% (October 2026), plus a premium for a leveraged bank with large government-bond holdings. Payout stays near 40%. In the base case, second-half EPS is similar to the first half's, less the tax and recovery one-offs, giving about Rs 31 for 2026.

Fair value and buy price
Fair value: weighting 30/50/20 gives about Rs 141 (0.85x NAV), so Rs 152 is about 8% above it.
Buy price: a 15% margin of safety gives Rs 120, and 25% gives Rs 106.
Plan for 500 shares: 200 at up to Rs 130, 150 at up to Rs 120 and 150 at up to Rs 110. That averages about Rs 121, about Rs 60,500, against Rs 76,000 at Rs 152.
Realism: this year's reported range is Rs 137.75–167.00 (first half of 2026), and the 2025 low was Rs 99.90. The first tier at Rs 130 needs about a 14% fall, and Rs 120 about 21%, which would need a broad market sell-off. A small starter at today's price yields about 6.8%, but it's above fair value.

Sensitivity (residual income base case, Rs per share)
Cost of equity 16%: 150.2 / 179.5 / 211.5 for long-run ROE of 14% / 16% / 18%.
Cost of equity 18%: 121.9 / 143.4 / 166.8.
Cost of equity 20%: 102.1 / 118.4 / 136.1.
Today's Rs 152 is only supported with a 16% cost of equity, or with an 18% cost of equity and a long-run ROE of 18%.

What would change my view
Supports a higher value: loan growth continuing while Stage 3 loans keep falling; the margin holding above 4.2%; lower interest rates, which would lower the cost of equity; ROE staying above 19%; cash dividends of Rs 12+ for 2026; Q3 results (due by mid-November) confirming the first half.
Supports a lower value: capital being used up by fast loan growth, leading to smaller cash dividends, a scrip dividend or a rights issue; a provisioning cycle (Stage 2 loans rose Rs 36.8bn); the first half's one-offs (tax settlement, recoveries, exchange gains) not repeating; rising rates squeezing margins and the bond portfolio; higher taxes on banks; stress in the government-bond market.

These are my estimates from the 2025 annual report and the 2025–2026 interim reports. The interim figures are unaudited, and the price is the CSE close of 6 November 2026, so check it before ordering. This is analysis, not personal financial advice.
